newsitem.title: UK: Britain eases Loyalists' talks expulsion fears.
newsitem.headline: Britain eases Loyalists' talks expulsion fears.

text.p: Britain said on Monday it was not seeking expulsion of Protestant Loyalist parties from Northern Ireland multi-party peace talks despite sectarian attacks blamed by police on Loyalist extremists.

Northern Ireland Office junior minister Michael Ancram told reporters before round-table talks were due to start he did not believe politicians linked to the banned extremists had breached peace principles underpinning their places at the talks.
"What we have to evaluate is whether the participants here, or any of them, have demonstrably dishonoured the...six Mitchell Principles to which they signed up at the beginning of this process.
"I do not believe that to be the case but obviously I will want to hear what other parties have to say this morning."
The Loyalist parties, the political wings of outlawed extremist groups, want Northern Ireland to remain British.

Sinn Fein, political wing of the guerrilla Irish Republican Army (IRA) which is fighting for the province to be united with Ireland, has been barred from the talks until the IRA reinstates the truce it ended last year with bombs on the British mainland.
Ancram stressed there could be no double standards and that Britain would continue to evaluate the position.

After a bomb attack on a Catholic family last week, Britain issued a stiff warning to Loyalist parties that representations might be made to have them thrown them out of talks if it was felt that they had breached peace principles.
Ancram said that "the evaluation we have made is not going to lead us to make a formal representation..."
Police chiefs blame Loyalist guerrillas for what they regard as revenge attacks after a surge in hostilities by the IRA.
But they have not publicly linked the incidents to the politicians' allies in the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC) which declared a ceasefire in October 1994.
Earlier, Loyalist politicians who say they want to see all violence ended said the CLMC was still holding to a ceasefire.

Critics of the Loyalists among mainstream Protestant parties said the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) and Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) should be expelled if it were established that the attacks were approved by the CLMC.

"Our indications are...that the CLMC are still very much committed to their ceasefire and that they are very much committed to seeing a peaceful democratic resolution of the problems within Northern Ireland," UDP politician David Adams told BBC radio before the talks.

The row added a new layer of controversy to the Anglo-Irish sponsored peace talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, that have been dogged by disputes and overshadowed by IRA violence since their launch last June.
